I don't know if you really grasp the magnitude of the difference between optical and solid state storage back in the late 90s when this battle was fought out.

A standard CD-ROM could store something around 650-700 MB, and a pressing of a disc only took a few cents comparatively speaking. Meanwhile, the size of the largest N64 game possible was somewhere around 64 MB, maximum, and cost a lot more since you were making chips - actual hardware. The inherent cost of the cartridges also increased with complexity - in fact, some NES and SNES cartridges carried pretty hefty upgrades on board, which had to be made uniquely for every last game that used them. The Super FX chip for SNES was a secondary processor that was more powerful than the SNES CPU - so every cartridge that used it had to have its own additional CPU just for it, that was more powerful than the core processor on the SNES. Not cheap, not at all, and that left a foul taste in the mouth of many consumers, especially when people were paying $70-80 a cart in some cases.

Why'd Nintendo go with cartridges, then? Two main reasons, not really including cost. First was a form of physical DRM, which didn't do all that much good but was better than CD-ROMs. The most important difference was speed. There were no loading screens with cartridges, or at least, not many. But the speed advantage could be worked around when you've got so much more storage available, especially when it's cheap enough that you can afford to have multiple pieces of game media available (hence why some games for other systems spanned multiple discs - that would have cost an arm and a leg). This is also why games like Final Fantasy 7 went straight to the Playstation.

There is a third reason they may have gone for it as well - control. Back in the days of the original NES, your entire fate was effectively at Nintendo's mercy. You ordered your carts from them, and you had to be happy with whatever they gave you, and you could only put out a few games per year. You were their bitch, and naturally they rather enjoyed that position. That weakened somewhat during the NES era, unsurprisingly. I don't know if that managed to persist into the N64 era, but it would be a fairly powerful incentive. Nintendo seems to have managed this to some extent with things like the discs used for the Game Cube being proprietary and such, but I don't know if they tried to force the issue like with the NES.

Nintendo's counter, the external disk drive, flopped in Japan, didn't store nearly as much as a CD, and also was a console accessory, which is a lot harder sell than the console itself. Adding $200 to a machine that's already $200-$250 is not going to make parents happy, after all. It didn't even make it to the US. So they really had almost everything crammed into a tiny, tiny space, in exchange for no loading screens. This also likely didn't make third party developers happy at all - the SNES CD-ROM add-on self-destructed and was recycled into the PlayStation, and the N64 disk drive, long touted as a wonderful add-on, never even made it to the states and collapsed spectacularly in Japan.

But the game has changed over the last 15 years. SSDs are cheap and plentiful to the point of being treated like floppy disks were once upon a time. Plus, having the console double as a CD/DVD/Blu Ray player is a lot less appealing than it was a few years ago. Now, optical media is more trouble than it's worth, so the NX switching to something like a cartridge is a lot more likely and logical.

let me explain why:

back in the day, there was about 10 times more space on a CD than on a diskette, which essentially a cartridge was. which is why games on the playstation, like crash bandicoot and tekken had WAY more impressive textures or music than mario64(which was either really plane colors or super low resolution stretched out blurrily billenearly textures): it had the space. but todays "cartridges" are literally discs inside a box, flash usb drives, sd cards, ssd's, hard drives.

so why are "cartridges" superior?

two words: enhancement chips.

an enhancement chip had the capability of either being something like extra ram or a small extra cpu or graphics chip, or it could have software along the hardware, to use the hardware on the system better, or even add more sound channels.

examples: the mode 7, scaling objects, and the moldable gooey boss were only possible on the SNES due to the "Super FX 2" chip.

and the 3d in star fox on the snes was only possible due to the original "Super FX" chip (earlier known as the "mario chip")

the amazing amounts of colour pallettes on backgrounds on characters in things like the zelda oracle series on gameboy color, or wario land 3 and so forth, was only possible due to the "MBC" (memory bank controller (used for bank switching for creatively using space more efficiently)), and the same was done with the MMC (memory management controller) on the NES in things like castlevania, specifically the VRC6 chip, which on the japanese famicom EVEN ADDED 3 MORE SOUND CHANNELS! (2 pulse, 1 sawtooth(which i personally think should have been a Wave channel instead, but oh well))

enhancement chips could even increase the amounts of objects per screen or scanline at once possible, or add more colors capable on the gameboy color (mode 3 mid-scanline rendering), by flashing colors so fast right after each other that they combined :P (used in very few games (it was pioneered by the italian game company "7th Sense") the games it was in: the new adams family (game boy colour) the fish files (game boy color)

it could also allow bigger sprites(which are just smaller objects put together :P), more colors (usually, only 4 colors per sprite, including transparent. meaning it would often be 1 dark(black or brown), one light (white or yellow) and one actual color(green, blue, red)). also, doing things such as allowing background tiles to have independent colors (usually they were bound to have the same colour in a 4X4 cell of 4X4 pixelled objects), which could make great cutscene or gallery pictures :P

in summary, having a cartridge these days allows both for tremendous space (tho you can always have your files on the memory card SD as backup, or install it on the machine, with updates), as well as adding extra software AND hardware, and having complete and direct control, modifying the system momentarily to be completely optimized for the game experience, pushing it to its very limits, getting every byte of memory and performance out of it :P (could even be used for small things like a microphone or camera upgrade)

the next step of this, would be giving the users the power :P it's cool that the developing houses can modify the machine again, but it would be revolutionary if you could change the parts of it, say a slight upgrade of cpu that wouldn't need you to buy an entire new system and let the old one sit in a museum (akin to the nintendo ds consoles...), as well as allowing some more of what made the playstation popular: modding and hacking :P modchips and piracy aside, the homebrews and the hacked/modded ps1's were awesome. essentially, it would keep the console alive well beyond its lifespan to have access to it's software and hardware (and it not being build in a difficult way), akin to how minecraft stayed alive for so long, due to user created content and mods, without mojang needing to do much for it :P or how mario maker essentially gives you the toolset to let loose. you get the point.
